chunks: Eye mask and mask violations. The question: What is the mask of an eye diagram? What happens if some of the signal enters the mask?
An eye mask is a pass/fail template drawn on the eye diagram. The standard for an interface defines a shape in the middle of the eye, plus limits above and below.
A compliant signal must never touch it. If any part of the signal's traces enters the mask, that is a mask violation and the signal fails the test.
Think of a cardboard cutout the shape of the smallest tunnel a truck must fit through. You hold it up in front of the real opening.
If the tunnel walls poke into the cutout anywhere, the truck does not fit. The mask works the same way for the eye: it is the smallest opening a compliant signal must leave.
Left: a healthy eye passes cleanly between the mask and the amplitude limits. Right: bigger jitter (edges shifted ±45 px, about ±0.
25 UI), slower edges and ISI droop push traces into the orange hexagon; each red dot is a mask hit. The dashed lines are top and bottom amplitude limits.
The mask shape and size are illustrative only.
Eye diagram: all the bits overlaid on one picture ("What an eye diagram shows"). Mask: the standard's polygons in the middle of the eye and above and below it.
Keep-out region: the central polygon that the signal must stay out of. Mask hit: a sample point that lands inside the mask.
Mask margin: how much bigger the mask could be made before the signal starts failing.
Suppose (made-up numbers for illustration) an interface's mask blocks out the middle 40% of the bit time and the middle 50% of the voltage swing.
A tester captures 1,000,000 bits of a test pattern, lays them over the eye, and counts how many points land inside the mask. Zero hits means a pass.
A hit may fail the test, depending on the standard. Now scale the mask up by 25% and run the count again. If there are still zero hits, the signal has 25% margin.
Hits at the left and right sides of the mask mean the eye is too narrow (jitter). Hits at the top and bottom mean it is too short.
That is the whole idea: a signal that clears the template passes.
"An eye mask is a pass/fail template overlaid on the eye: a hexagon or rectangle in the middle plus limits above and below, defined by the standard in normalised time and voltage.
A compliant signal keeps out of it.
If some of the signal enters the mask, that's a violation, a hit: the signal doesn't give enough margin in voltage or timing, so it fails compliance.
Where the hits are tells you whether it's jitter, noise or ISI, and you fix that and check the mask margin."
